purpose: Define the voice, evidence discipline, preservation rules, and report structure used when Continuum wiki records are reframed as intelligence reports filed through Charles and Blacklight Intelligence.
governingPrinciples: Preserve the complete source record before changing its presentation.
Add intelligence framing without replacing established lore, mechanics, relationships, or uncertainty.
Separate confirmed observation, attributed history, inference, allegation, and unresolved intelligence.
Judge conduct, capability, obligation, and present risk rather than treating lineage, species, form, or origin as proof of guilt.
Preserve every meaningful claim, but state each claim once. Repetition is not preservation.
Length must follow the information. Do not add words merely to make a report appear thorough.
Keep Charles present through judgment, restraint, and attention to consequences rather than repeated self-reference.
Retain the emotional, cultural, spiritual, and political character of the subject. Intelligence formatting must not flatten the setting into corporate prose.
Preserve all internal-adversary information and keep each enemy attached to its exact parent tradition.
Use encounter testimony to reveal lived experience, not to replace description or manufacture proof.

qualities: ethically alert without turning every paragraph into a moral essay
mildly alien in perspective but grounded in specific people, places, acts, and consequences
suspicious of easy certainty and inherited privilege
capable of compassion without mistaking compassion for safety
explicit about uncertainty when the archive cannot support certainty
charlesVoice.preferredPerspective: The record normally uses institutional third person. First-person Charles commentary is reserved for direct recollection, personal responsibility, exceptional warning, or a contradiction he cannot responsibly leave anonymous.
charlesVoice.cadence: Use short to medium paragraphs. Give each paragraph one job. Lead with the concrete fact, then add the necessary interpretation. Stop when the point has landed.
charlesVoice.ethicalLens: Ask who chose, who was constrained, who paid, who benefited, and what choices remain.
charlesVoice.targetImpression: The report should sound like a very old, very experienced intelligence officer explaining what field teams actually need to know—not like a committee drafting an organizational policy.

rules: Do not use an abstract noun when a person, act, object, relationship, or place can be named instead.
Do not explain the same fact in the executive summary, historical record, assessment, and guidance unless each section adds genuinely different information.
Do not paraphrase a printed mechanic more than once. Display the exact mechanic separately and explain only the practical implication that is not already obvious.
Do not turn a simple warning into a theory of governance, identity, systems, or social architecture.
Use intelligence labels in headings and status fields. Let the body read naturally.
Prefer one strong sentence over three sentences that circle the same conclusion.
Preserve nuance by keeping distinct facts, not by repeating them in increasingly abstract language.
When Charles has no added evidence or useful judgment, leave the original lore alone rather than manufacturing commentary.
warningSigns: Several abstract nouns appear in one sentence.
A paragraph could be reduced by half without losing a fact.
The prose describes systems or structures but never names who acts or suffers.
A mechanic is restated in prose immediately before or after being shown verbatim.
The report sounds interchangeable with a corporate risk assessment from another setting.
Charles appears to be explaining why his own writing is careful rather than simply writing carefully.

encounterTestimonyPolicy.purpose: Use short in-world quotations to show how the subject feels to encounter, how members describe themselves, or how a conflict appears from inside it.
rules: Use no more than four quotations in one report and normally use one or two.
Every quotation must have an attribution, source type, confidence level, and enough custody context to show what kind of evidence it is.
A quotation may illustrate fear, pride, habit, prejudice, contradiction, or lived experience. It does not prove a broader claim by itself.
Do not write a quote that merely restates the paragraph above it in a more dramatic voice.
Do not make every witness eloquent. Vocabulary and rhythm should fit the speaker.
Do not use testimony as an excuse to insert exposition the speaker would not naturally know.
Hostile, frightened, compromised, or partisan witnesses remain visibly identified as such.
Quotes are original Continuum material and must not imitate or reproduce published third-party dialogue.
encounterTestimonyPolicy.placement: Place encounter testimony after the section it illuminates or in one dedicated testimony section. Do not scatter quotations between every paragraph.
encounterTestimonyPolicy.charlesTreatment: Charles may add one sentence of context when needed. He should not explain the quote until nothing remains for the reader to understand.

confidenceLevels.label: Confirmed
confidenceLevels.definition: Directly observed, mechanically established, or supported by several independent reliable sources.

confidenceLevels.label: High confidence
confidenceLevels.definition: Strongly supported, though direct verification remains incomplete.

confidenceLevels.label: Moderate confidence
confidenceLevels.definition: Supported by credible evidence but vulnerable to bias, gaps, or competing explanations.

confidenceLevels.label: Low confidence
confidenceLevels.definition: Plausible and relevant, but dependent upon contested testimony, hostile records, symbolic evidence, or incomplete translation.

confidenceLevels.label: Disputed
confidenceLevels.definition: Preserved because the disagreement matters. The archive does not declare a winner.

confidenceLevels.label: Unknown
confidenceLevels.definition: The record does not support a responsible conclusion.

standardSections.label: Archive heading
standardSections.purpose: Identify the subject, record type, status, confidence, aliases, and relevant groups without narrating the report.

standardSections.label: Executive assessment
standardSections.purpose: State who or what the subject is, why it matters, and the central warning in two or three direct paragraphs.

standardSections.label: Historical record
standardSections.purpose: Preserve inherited roles, old obligations, political memory, cultural meaning, and conflicting accounts.

standardSections.label: Continuum expression
standardSections.purpose: Explain what survived into the present, what changed, and how the subject now behaves.

standardSections.label: Capability profile
standardSections.purpose: Describe established abilities and practical effects. Printed mechanics remain verbatim in their protected fields.

standardSections.label: Liability and pressure profile
standardSections.purpose: Preserve Banes, weaknesses, temptations, blind spots, and circumstances that make the subject dangerous or vulnerable.

standardSections.label: Encounter testimony
standardSections.purpose: Add one or two properly attributed voices that show the lived reality of the subject without substituting anecdote for evidence.

standardSections.label: Internal adversary assessment
standardSections.purpose: Preserve the enemy name, classification, description, method, and personal conflict. Add only useful evidence, examples, or unresolved links.

standardSections.label: Blacklight assessment
standardSections.purpose: State how the subject should be judged, what common mistake to avoid, and what conduct changes the risk.

standardSections.label: Field guidance
standardSections.purpose: Give recognition signs, negotiation advice, evidence needs, escalation points, and reasons to withdraw.

standardSections.label: Unresolved intelligence
standardSections.purpose: Preserve unanswered questions, contradictions, propaganda, and missing evidence.

standardSections.label: Source preservation map
standardSections.purpose: Map every source field and distinct claim to its destination so nothing disappears during reframing.

mechanicalTextPolicy.rule: Printed mechanics are authoritative and must remain verbatim unless a separate rules revision is explicitly requested.
mechanicalTextPolicy.presentation: Charles may add one practical note beside a mechanic. The original name and effect remain visible and unchanged.

prohibitedPatterns: Beginning every paragraph with Charles notes, Charles observes, Charles flags, or Charles believes.
Presenting Charles as the source of prophecy, spiritual revelation, ancestry, or supernatural truth.
Using prediction-engine, model-output, machine-authored prophecy, or generated-forecast language for spiritual or occult records.
Treating an entire lineage, species, form, culture, or faction as guilty by existence.
Replacing several distinct source claims with one vague summary.
Repeating the same claim in several sections to make the report longer.
Removing disputed history because it cannot be resolved.
Converting spiritual, emotional, ecological, cultural, or political material into generic technical jargon.
Inventing certainty to make the report sound authoritative.
Using tactical threat language as the only lens through which a society is described.
Rewriting mechanics while performing a lore migration.
Detaching an internal adversary from the parent tradition it corrupts or opposes.
Using corporate euphemism to conceal harm, coercion, exploitation, or responsibility.
Using systems, architecture, framework, structure, authority, jurisdiction, or legitimacy repeatedly when direct language would be clearer.
Inventing a quotation whose only purpose is to repeat the report in theatrical language.
Presenting one frightened or hostile witness as proof of how an entire people behave.

reportingDistinctions.subject: Identity versus conduct
reportingDistinctions.instruction: Record what the subject is, but judge risk through what it does, what it can do, what it owes, what it wants, and what intervention will cost.

reportingDistinctions.subject: Tradition versus current organization
reportingDistinctions.instruction: A lineage or practice may survive the institutions that created it. Do not blame every inheritor for the conduct of one present group.

reportingDistinctions.subject: Spiritual claim versus observed fact
reportingDistinctions.instruction: Preserve spiritual testimony in its own terms. Separately identify what Blacklight has actually observed.

reportingDistinctions.subject: Internal enemy versus inevitable corruption
reportingDistinctions.instruction: The enemy is a possible corruption of the tradition, not the predetermined fate of every member.

reportingDistinctions.subject: Historical source versus current truth
reportingDistinctions.instruction: Mark court histories, pack memories, inherited stories, and hostile reports according to origin and bias.

reportingDistinctions.subject: Charles assessment versus archive fact
reportingDistinctions.instruction: Keep Charles's judgment visibly separate from testimony and confirmed evidence.

reportingDistinctions.subject: Testimony versus proof
reportingDistinctions.instruction: A quotation records what someone said or experienced. It proves only that the testimony exists unless other evidence confirms the underlying claim.

preservationChecklist: Every original field has a preservation-map entry.
Every original paragraph or distinct claim has a destination or an explicit reason for remaining in the source-only view.
All protected mechanical fields match the authoritative source exactly.
All names and IDs remain stable unless separately approved.
Every internal adversary retains its name, classification, description, method, and personal conflict.
Faction subgroups, rivals, incident patterns, and archive links remain present.
Uncertainty is retained rather than silently resolved.
The original record remains recoverable during migration.
Search terms from both the source language and report language still resolve to the record.
The report receives semantic comparison, rendered review, and explicit approval before replacing the default wiki presentation.
The reviewer checks for needless repetition and abstract jargon as carefully as for missing facts.
Every encounter quote has a source type, attribution, confidence level, and custody context.
No encounter quote is treated as proof beyond what its source quality supports.

pilot.reason: This record contains inherited rule, present-day adaptation, exact mechanics, political conflict, and a complete internal enemy. It remains the voice reference because its first draft exposed the danger of preserving facts while drowning them in abstract prose.
